summary: ENUM domain names are tied to E.164 telephone numbers, so one must check that the registrant of an ENUM domain is also the assignee of the number. This informational document describes the requirements and a high-level architecture for that validation infrastructure.

plainLanguage.summary: Before someone can put a phone number into the internet's phone book, someone should check it is really theirs. This describes how that checking could work.

subtitle: Ensuring that ENUM domain registrants actually own the phone numbers they register.

tldr.problem: ENUM maps E.164 phone numbers to domain names in the DNS so calls can be routed using internet resources. But anyone could register an ENUM domain for someone else's phone number if there is no validation, causing fraud and service disruption.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines roles and a workflow for validation: a Validation Entity checks that the person registering an ENUM domain (the Registrant) is the same person or organization who was assigned that phone number (the Assignee), and performs both initial and recurring re-validation throughout the domain's lifetime.
tldr.outcome: When validation is properly implemented, only the rightful phone number holder can register the corresponding ENUM domain, preventing hijacking and maintaining the integrity of the ENUM namespace.

facts.label: Phone number standard
facts.value: E.164, administered by the International Telecommunication Union (ITU)

facts.label: Typical re-validation interval
facts.value: Set by local ENUM administration policy (commonly 1-5 years)

today: RFC 4725 is Informational and describes an architecture for ENUM validation. ENUM deployments vary by country; some have implemented formal validation while others remain in trial phases. The RFC remains the foundational document for understanding how validation should work in ENUM systems.

sections.title: The Link Between ENUM and E.164 Numbers
sections.content:
ENUM (E.164 Number Mapping) uses the DNS to allow a phone number to be looked up and translated into a web address or service identifier. Unlike a regular domain name, which is allocated on a first-come-first-served basis, an ENUM domain name is tightly coupled to an E.164 telephone number. This coupling creates a critical requirement: the person registering the ENUM domain must be the person or organization to whom that phone number was assigned.

Without proper validation, an attacker could register the ENUM domain for someone else's phone number. This could be used for "man in the middle" attacks (for example, intercepting calls meant for a bank) or simple fraud.
sections.plainLanguage: A phone number is yours, assigned by a phone company. Your ENUM entry should only exist if you say so, to prevent someone else from hijacking your phone number on the internet.

sections.title: Roles in the ENUM System
sections.content:
The RFC defines several key roles. The Number Assignment Entity (NAE) is the organization (usually a phone company) that assigns phone numbers to users. The Assignee is the person or organization who holds the phone number. The Registrant is the person who controls the ENUM domain name. For proper function, the Assignee and Registrant must be the same entity.

The Validation Entity (VE) verifies this match. The Registrar coordinates with the Validation Entity and then submits the domain registration to the Registry, which operates the authoritative ENUM database. The DNS Service Provider (DNS-SP) runs the nameservers, and the Application Service Provider (ASP) provides services to Registrants (such as call routing).

A single organization may perform multiple roles, or the roles may be completely separated depending on local policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone company (NAE) assigns numbers, the validator (VE) checks ownership, the registrar handles paperwork, the registry keeps the master list, and the DNS provider serves it on the internet.

sections.title: Initial and Recurring Validation
sections.content:
When someone orders an ENUM domain, the Registrar requests validation from a Validation Entity. The VE checks that (1) the number is assigned and within approved ranges, (2) the requester is authorized by the Assignee, and (3) the Registrant is the Assignee. Initial validation may involve contacting the NAE's subscriber database, or even calling the number to confirm the user's intention.

Validation does not happen once and end. The RFC requires recurring validation (re-validation) at regular intervals, typically set by local ENUM administration policy. During re-validation the VE confirms that the requirements still hold. If re-validation fails, the ENUM domain delegation must be suspended from the DNS, ensuring that stale or unauthorized entries disappear.

This ongoing process maintains the integrity between the E.164 namespace and the ENUM namespace, even as phone numbers are reassigned or users change providers.
sections.plainLanguage: The validator checks once when you register, and checks again periodically to make sure you still own the number and want the ENUM entry.

sections.title: Trust Relationships and Data Exchange
sections.content:
The validation architecture creates trust relationships. The Registry must trust that Registrars and Validation Entities enforce the validation policy correctly. Registrars must trust Validation Entities to accurately perform validation. Validation Entities must be trusted to access NAE subscriber databases securely and confidentially.

Data flows between multiple parties. Registrars communicate with Validation Entities to initiate validation and receive results. If the local policy requires, Validation Entities communicate with NAEs to verify number assignment. The Registry may receive validation-related metadata (such as an expiry date or a cryptographic signature from the VE) along with the registration, providing additional assurance.

When validation data carries cryptographic signatures, the Registry can independently verify authenticity without trusting intermediaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Each player trusts the others to do their job right: the validator trusts the phone company's database, the registry trusts the validator's answer, and rules about who sees which data protect privacy.

sections.title: Practical Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
The RFC describes two example scenarios. In the first, an Internet Telephony Service Provider (ITSP) acts as all three roles: NAE (assigns numbers), Registrar (handles registration), and Validation Entity (checks against its own subscriber database). This simplifies the process: when a customer orders a new phone number and ENUM domain at once, the ITSP immediately knows the assignment is valid and can proceed to registration.

The second scenario is more complex: roles are fully separated. The NAE is a national numbering authority. A separate Registrar handles registration, and a separate Validation Entity performs checking. The VE must query the NAE's database and may even call the number to verify the user's intention. While more complex to orchestrate, this model provides independence and can prevent conflicts of interest.
sections.plainLanguage: A small phone company can do all the work itself: assign, validate, and register. A big system needs different companies for each job and they have to coordinate carefully.
